title: Swap the Curve
subtitle: observed against expected, at a reference clinic
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E11_SwapTheCurve
status: DRAFT: script under review together with its animatic.

segments.visual: Alder's 30 patients as chips: 24 lower-risk, 6 higher-risk, 13 of them filled. Then Episode 3's two answers: 1.4 and 1.8.

sentences.text: Alder had 13 readmissions among its 30 patients. Is that a lot?
sentences.say: Alder had thirteen readmissions among its thirty patients. Is that a lot?

sentences.text: In Episode 3 we got two answers. Against everyone pooled together, 1.4 times what was expected. Against everyone but Alder itself, 1.8.
sentences.say: In Episode three we got two answers. Against everyone pooled together, one point four times what was expected. Against everyone but Alder itself, one point eight.

segments.visual: Episode 3's two requirements as two cards: a risk rule learned inside clinics, ticked, with the dial's symbol beside it; a yardstick no single clinic can bend, marked today.

sentences.text: So we asked for two things: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic, and a yardstick no single clinic can bend.
The risk rule arrived with the dial. Today, the yardstick.

segments.visual: Alder's chips on the left, an empty grey frame labelled the middle clinic on the right, an arrow between them and a question: more than 13, or fewer?

sentences.text: Here is the idea. Keep Alder's 30 patients exactly as they are, and send them, on paper, to the middle clinic.
sentences.say: Here is the idea. Keep Alder's thirty patients exactly as they are, and send them, on paper, to the middle clinic.

sentences.text: Would they have more than 13 readmissions there, or fewer?
sentences.say: Would they have more than thirteen readmissions there, or fewer?

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: swap the curve.

segments.visual: A log-odds ruler with the five clinics. Elm's marker is hatched, far to the left. A line marks the middle one: Cedar, at −1.52.

sentences.text: First, the yardstick. Line up the five sliders, and take the one in the middle.
It is Cedar's, at minus 1.52. And as we saw last time, it stays put wherever Elm's slider happens to stop.
sentences.say: It is Cedar's, at minus one point five two. And as we saw last time, it stays put wherever Elm's slider happens to stop.

segments.visual: The probability panel with one grey curve: the reference. Two risk chips on it: 18% at the lower-risk end, 62% at the higher-risk end.

sentences.text: Draw that clinic's curve in grey, and call it the reference.
At the reference, a lower-risk patient has an 18% chance of readmission. A higher-risk patient, 62%.
sentences.say: At the reference, a lower-risk patient has an eighteen percent chance of readmission. A higher-risk patient, sixty-two percent.

segments.visual: A note beside the curve: a clinic, not an average patient.

sentences.text: Notice what kind of thing the reference is. Not an average patient. A clinic: one clinic's level, applied to whoever walks in.

segments.visual: Alder's curve in its own colour above the grey one. Two risk chips on Alder's curve: 24 patients at 34%, 6 at 80%. The sum: 24 × 0.343 + 6 × 0.796 = 13.0.

sentences.text: Here are Alder's patients on Alder's own curve: 24 lower-risk patients at 34%, and 6 higher-risk at 80%.
sentences.say: Here are Alder's patients on Alder's own curve: twenty-four lower-risk patients at thirty-four percent, and six higher-risk at eighty percent.

sentences.text: Add up those chances, and you get 13. Exactly what Alder observed, because the fit balanced it.
sentences.say: Add up those chances, and you get thirteen. Exactly what Alder observed, because the fit balanced it.

segments.visual: Both chips drop straight down onto the grey curve, and their slices shrink to 18% and 62%. The sum: 24 × 0.179 + 6 × 0.621 = 8.02.

sentences.text: Now swap the curve. The same 30 patients, on the grey one: 24 at 18%, and 6 at 62%.
sentences.say: Now swap the curve. The same thirty patients, on the grey one: twenty-four at eighteen percent, and six at sixty-two percent.

sentences.text: Add those up: 8.02.
sentences.say: Add those up: eight point zero two.

segments.visual: Observed 13 over expected 8.02, equals 1.62.

sentences.text: So at the reference, these same patients would expect about 8 readmissions. At Alder, there were 13.
sentences.say: So at the reference, these same patients would expect about eight readmissions. At Alder, there were thirteen.

sentences.text: 13 over 8.02 is 1.62. Alder had 62% more readmissions than its own patients would be expected to have at the reference clinic.
sentences.say: Thirteen over eight point zero two is one point six two. Alder had sixty-two percent more readmissions than its own patients would be expected to have at the reference clinic.

segments.visual: Three steps in a row: keep the patients, swap the curve, count.

sentences.text: That is the whole method. Keep the patients. Swap the curve. Count.

segments.visual: A ratio axis from 0 to 2 with a line at 1. Five markers: 1.62, 0.88, 1.00, 1.46 and 0.

sentences.text: Do the same for every clinic. Alder, 1.62. Birch, 0.88. Cedar, exactly 1. Dune, 1.46. And Elm, zero.
sentences.say: Do the same for every clinic. Alder, one point six two. Birch, zero point eight eight. Cedar, exactly one. Dune, one point four six. And Elm, zero.

sentences.text: Cedar comes out at exactly 1, because it is the reference, measured against itself.
sentences.say: Cedar comes out at exactly one, because it is the reference, measured against itself.

segments.visual: Alder's row gains Episode 3's two answers as hollow markers, 1.4 and 1.8. Then the ruler of sliders returns: one slider is pushed far away, and the middle marker moves only to the next clinic.

sentences.text: So Alder's answer is neither 1.4 nor 1.8. It is 1.62.
sentences.say: So Alder's answer is neither one point four nor one point eight. It is one point six two.

sentences.text: And this yardstick is hard to bend. Push any one slider as far as you like, and the middle value moves no further than the next clinic along.

segments.visual: Two totals beside the observed 42: expected counts add up to 42.0 against the pooled standard, and to 38.8 against the middle clinic.

sentences.text: One thing has changed since Episode 3. Against the pooled standard, the expected counts added up to the 42 observed. Against the middle clinic, they add up to 38.8.
sentences.say: One thing has changed since Episode three. Against the pooled standard, the expected counts added up to the forty-two observed. Against the middle clinic, they add up to thirty-eight point eight.

sentences.text: The clinics no longer break even as a group, and they need not.

segments.visual: Each ratio times the overall rate, 41%. Five bars: 66%, 36%, 41%, 59% and 0%, with a line at 41%.

sentences.text: Ratios are often reported as rates. Multiply each one by the overall readmission rate, 41%.
sentences.say: Ratios are often reported as rates. Multiply each one by the overall readmission rate, forty-one percent.

sentences.text: Alder becomes 66%. Birch, 36. Cedar, 41. Dune, 59. Elm, zero.
sentences.say: Alder becomes sixty-six percent. Birch, thirty-six. Cedar, forty-one. Dune, fifty-nine. Elm, zero.

segments.visual: Alder's 66% beside the two chances its patients really have, 34% and 80%. A note: the same ratio, rescaled.

sentences.text: Read these with care. No patient at Alder had a 66% chance of readmission. It is the same ratio, moved to a more familiar scale.
sentences.say: Read these with care. No patient at Alder had a sixty-six percent chance of readmission. It is the same ratio, moved to a more familiar scale.

segments.visual: A curve: Alder's ratio against the position of its slider. Two points on it: 1 at the reference, 1.62 at Alder's own gamma.

sentences.text: One more connection. Move Alder's slider, and its ratio traces a single rising curve.
With the slider at the reference, the ratio is 1. At Alder's own gamma, 1.62.
sentences.say: With the slider at the reference, the ratio is one. At Alder's own gamma, one point six two.

segments.visual: Episode 9's interval on the slider axis, −1.50 to 0.19, carried up through the curve to the ratio axis: 1.02 to 2.31.

sentences.text: So every statement about a gamma becomes a statement about a ratio. Episode 9's interval for Alder's gamma becomes an interval for its ratio: from 1.02 to 2.31.
sentences.say: So every statement about a gamma becomes a statement about a ratio. Episode nine's interval for Alder's gamma becomes an interval for its ratio: from one point zero two to two point three one.

segments.visual: The ratio axis with its line at 1, labelled: like the reference clinic. Not a grade.

sentences.text: Two cautions. First, a ratio of 1 means like the reference clinic. It does not mean good.
sentences.say: Two cautions. First, a ratio of one means like the reference clinic. It does not mean good.

segments.visual: Alder's ratio under two references: 1.62 against the middle clinic, 1.87 against the size-weighted average.

sentences.text: Second, always say which reference. Last time we tried a size-weighted average instead of the middle clinic. Against that, Alder's 1.62 becomes 1.87.
sentences.say: Second, always say which reference. Last time we tried a size-weighted average instead of the middle clinic. Against that, Alder's one point six two becomes one point eight seven.

segments.visual: The crowd: 200 ratios as dots along the axis, from 0.44 to 1.99, half on each side of 1.

sentences.text: In our crowd of 200 providers, the ratios run from 0.44 to 1.99, with half on each side of 1.
sentences.say: In our crowd of two hundred providers, the ratios run from zero point four four to one point nine nine, with half on each side of one.

sentences.text: Which of those are real differences, and which are luck? That question is coming.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
The reference is the middle clinic's curve.
Keep a clinic's patients, swap in that curve, and count: observed over expected.
And name the reference with every ratio.

segments.visual: Two small pictures side by side: the same patients under a new curve; new patients under the same curve. The next episode's title.

sentences.text: We kept the patients and swapped the curve. Next time, the other way round: keep the curve, and swap the patients.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
